Concerning Animals, folio 2.

It has a large head; the ears are small; the snout is thick, fleshy, and short, and dark in color; its haunches are fatty; it has a broad face; its eyes are bright like burning coals; its fangs are large and thick; its teeth are small, little, and sharp; the molars wide at the top; and the mouth very wide; and it has long, sharp claws; it has thick necks on the forelegs and on the hind legs; and it has a white chest; it has a bright chest, and as it grows it becomes spotted, and its claws grow, and likewise its teeth grow, and its molars and fangs; and it snarls and bites and tears with its teeth and cuts; it growls, and roars making a sound like a trumpet.

The white tiger: they say it is the captain of the other tigers and is very white. There are others that are whitish, spotted with black.

There is another tiger of [long] hair

[Right column — Nahuatl text describing physical and behavioral attributes of the ocelot, its sounds, movements, and color variants:]

It is rough-eared, thick-lipped, thick-nosed, stout-snouted, hard-snouted, with folded jowls, with folds on its cheeks; flat-faced, with a rough face; with a smooth jaw, marked with black, spotted, speckled; ocelot-colored, curled, rolling about in curled fashion, curling itself, rolling about like an ocelot; it crouches, it compresses itself, it springs up, it rises up coiling like a serpent, it bounds, it leaps about, it tears apart, it crackles, it cries out, it screams, it sounds like a trumpet.

The white ocelot: they say it is the leader of the ocelots; it is white and very white. Some say we cannot catch it; it is spotted, it is marked with black, it leaps upward.

The red ocelot: it is very red, very tawny, all spotted,

Book Eleven

...red and spotted with black.

¶The nature of the tiger [jaguar] is that it eats animals, such as deer and rabbits and other similar creatures. It is fastidious and not suited for labor; it takes great care to keep itself clean; and at night it can see the animals it is going to hunt — it has very keen sight, and even if it is very dark, or even if there is fog, it can see very small things.
When it sees the hunter with his bow and arrows, it does not flee, but rather sits looking at him, without hiding behind anything or pressing up against anything. Then it begins to hiss, and that breath it directs toward the hunter, in order to instill fear and dread in him and make his heart faint with the hissing. And the hunter then begins to shoot at it; and the first arrow, which is made of cane, the jaguar catches with its paw and breaks it to pieces with its teeth, and begins to snarl and growl, and as another arrow is shot at it...

[Nahuatl column:]
¶This is how it lives: the ocelot goes about seeking, pursuing, those it will eat — deer, rabbits, etc. And it is very fastidious: it is not crude; it is very refined, it grooms itself, it washes itself, it cleans its face, it licks itself; it is deceptive, boastful; it is very alert, it is very prepared. And with its sight it looks at, it observes, what it seeks to eat, what it hunts; it sees very well, its gaze is sharp and clear, seeing well at a distance: even in darkness, even in dimness, it sees. When it sees, when it encounters, when it faces its adversary — it does not lower its head, it does not look down; it stands facing it squarely. It settles itself well, it crouches for nothing — the jaguar. Then it begins to snort, to blow its breath, so as to terrify the hunter, to make his heart stop, the one shooting at it. And then the hunter begins to shoot at it; one arrow that he launches — of cane — the jaguar simply catches it and pulls it and snaps it apart, and slaps at it...

Concerning animals                    fo. 3

He does the same. The hunters kept the custom that they were not to shoot the jaguar more than four arrows: this was their tradition or devotion. And if they did not kill it with those four arrows, the hunter would consider himself defeated. And the jaguar then begins to stretch itself, and to shake itself, and to lick itself. Having done this, it gathers itself and leaps as if flying, and throws itself upon the hunter. Even if the hunter is ten or twenty fathoms away, it takes but one leap; it goes all bristled up, like a cat against a dog. Then it kills the hunter and eats him. Skilled hunters, upon shooting the first arrow — if the jaguar was not shattered by it — take a leaf from an oak tree, and from another similar tree, and fix it onto the arrow, and shoot the jaguar with it. The leaf placed thus makes a sound, just as when a grasshopper flies and falls to the ground halfway, or nearby.

[Nahuatl column:] Making noises with its throat, snarling, it becomes enraged, as it is said. It throws itself at him just as many times as it shoots arrows at him, doing so in the same manner. And if the count of arrows shot at it falls short, even by one, the arrow flies: then it looks at the hunter. At dawn it yawns, stretches, shakes, quivers, cleans itself, flutters its sides. Then it truly readies itself; it stretches out its claws and flies off — ten measures away, the arrow stands erect in the air; even to the far side, twenty measures: it goes seizing it, for once it leaps: it flies, curves, circles around, surrounds — there the arrow dies; there it is consumed. And when it recovers: the hunter shoots another arrow, takes a reed, pulls it toward himself the quauhxiuatlapalli [eagle-herb board], and places the reed-tip there, and the reed comes out singing. He shoots it again, and it rustles as it goes: the acazoatl reed. Just as a grasshopper goes: perhaps it strikes the ground, perhaps it lands beside it, flying, falling, into the quauhxiuatlapalli: it cures its eyes with it.

Of Animals                                                    folio 4.

which is small, the size of a cat: it is brown, has some dark spots like a tiger or painted animal.

There is an animal in this land called tlacaxolotl: it is large, bigger than a great ox, it has a large head, a long snout, very wide ears, it has large teeth and molars: but in the form of a person, it has a very thick and sturdy neck, it has thick feet and hands, hooves like an ox but larger: it has large and wide haunches, its tail is thick and long: it is the color of a red ox, it has very thick hide: its meat is edible: they say its meat and flavor contains that of all animals, roots, and even of men. This animal is rare, it lives in the provinces of Atzaccan, and of Tepuztontlan, and Tlanguylapan, which are toward Honduras, it lives in the mountains and in certain places among the cliffs: it eats wild peanuts.

Tlacaxolotl, it greatly surpasses the cow: its head is very large and long-necked: its flesh is very thick and meaty: its teeth are very large: it appears roughly person-like, its neck is very thick and very fleshy: its shin, its leg, its body is very hairy and rough, very large, its mane is rough and shaggy, not smooth: its snout very large, its tail very thick, very long, not easily cut: its hair all over is not very long, like a deer's hair: its hide is dark-colored. This tlacaxolotl eats many things: and the flavor of its flesh is not in one part only — it has the taste of all kinds of meat: of human meat, of wild beast meat, of deer, of turkey, of dog. This tlacaxolotl, it lives only midway between — it dwells in Atzaccan, Tepuztontlan, Tlangutylapan, there in the great forest where no one can reach the interior. When it feeds it [illegible] when...

Book Eleven

These are the cacahuates called quappatlachtli. It also eats green corn and corn cobs. When it comes upon a cornfield, it eats everything, leaving nothing behind. When food is scarce, it eats the leaves of shrubs and trees. When it defecates, it expels the cacao beans whole, nearly a jarful of them each time. The inhabitants of that land go searching for its dung in order to collect the cacao it has passed. This animal does not fear people, nor does it die from an arrow. They catch it by digging a large pit and covering it with branches and grass so that it falls in; there they kill it, and from there they pull it out with ropes and eat its flesh, which is very good to eat.

And it cries out among the trees in the forest. When it finds nothing to eat, this animal called Jeucacaoatl, also quappatlahtli, goes to the cornfields and takes corn one ear at a time. It scatters the cacao, and it is good at carrying loads on its back. The commoners go looking for it in the forest so that they can collect the cacao from it. It is not timid, nor does it die from arrows, even if it is wounded. It does not dig burrows; it goes all about searching among the stones and rocks, and it goes far into the woods. When they have found it, they lay logs and stones over it and cover it.

Concerning animals. Folio 5.

[Spanish, left column:]
There is an animal called tzonistac. It is found toward the South Sea, in the province of Toztlan and Casepan. It is called tzonistac because it has a very white head only. It is about the size of a tiger, more or less. It is low to the ground and thick-bodied. It eats the flesh of wild beasts. When it wishes to hunt, it snarls like a cat and then suddenly seizes its prey. It has hands and feet like a tiger. Its entire body is very black, and it has a long tail. This animal

[Nahuatl, upper right:]
there: and then it goes and twists itself upon the person there, it tears him apart, and thus he dies there; then afterwards it drags him away with its mouth.

[Nahuatl, lower right:]
Tzonistac: it is a beast of prey. It lives over there in Tozllantzapan, somewhat near the great sea. The reason it is called tzonistac is that its head is very white, and it is white down to the neck; it is quite large in body, about the size of an ocelot — somewhat thick, somewhat flat. It goes about stalking the animals that roam about. When it sees them, it immediately growls loudly, it gnashes its teeth; then it leaps upon them; then, just like an ocelot, it is very agile, flying through the air upon them.

Book Eleven

It appears very rarely; and if someone encounters it and sees that its head is yellow, it is a sign that he will die soon. And if someone encounters it and its head appears white, it is a sign that he will live long in poverty even though he works very hard. This omen was associated with this animal: they kill it with an arrow.

[Nahuatl column:]
Its entire body is shining and glistening; its tail is long, just as that of the ocelot. And if one sees it with a white head, no one can look upon whoever encounters it; if one who sees it does not become ill from the encounter — then that person will live a very long time, will endure long, though he suffers greatly; and even more so it is said: if such and such conditions are met, and in such a way it is received, whoever eats of the animal's broth thereby gains something, for it reaches and overtakes them.

Of Animals. Folio 6.

[partial Nahuatl text at top, partially illegible]

This animal, by its description, appears to be a bear; and if it is not a bear, I do not know what animal among those we know it can be compared to. It is a hairy animal, with long wool: it has a tail, very woolly, like that of a fox; but of a dark brownish color, it has shaggy wool; when it is old: it has small, narrow ears; it has a round face, wide, almost like that of a person; it has a thick snout; it has a little gland for being venomous, to poison whatever it encounters; the vapor or air that it emits is of many colors, like a rainbow; it is very cunning, and lies in ambush to kill.

The lion: it is the size of a tiger, it is not spotted; it also has sleek fur; and in body it is like a tiger, except that it has larger claws, and also small ones very long; it is rarely dark; there are red lions and others whitish: these are called white lions.

Cujtlachtli [the bear/wolverine]: or also called cueclachtli; it is thick, rounded, very large, with a broad tail base, [its tail hairs spread out]; its [fur] is very rounded and smooth; it cannot [easily] be compared to our [animals]; it is somewhat like a chichimec person in appearance, very large and broad; it is very round-faced, very clear-eyed, it sees those who approach it; it is just like a rainbow coming from its mouth; it is very knowing, it can imitate people and make itself known; it rolls upon people, it makes itself known, it causes flatulence.

Miztli [the mountain lion/puma]: it is just like the ocelot in size and appearance: there is nothing that can be placed alongside it; it is entirely slender, narrow, exactly alike, very long and lean, very lean and straight; it leaps very well, it is dark-smoked in color; the reddish puma is tawny-colored; the [other kind of] puma — in some [accounts] it is called the white puma.

Book Eleven

¶This animal, which is called the quaumiztli [tree-lion/ocelot], by its properties appears to be an onza [lynx/wildcat]. And if it is not one, no other animal seems so similar: they say it resembles a lion, except that it always lives in the trees, leaping from branch to branch, and there it seeks its food. It rarely comes down to the ground.

¶There is an animal in these parts called the maçamiztli [deer-lion]. The name means a certain kind of lion. It is not known whether it exists anywhere else. It is the size of a deer, and has the color of a deer, and has claws like a deer's, and the males have horns like a deer; but it has feet like a lion, very sharp, and teeth and fangs like a lion. It does not eat plants. It lives among the other deer. And when it wants to eat, it embraces a deer and grips it by the neck; it opens it through the belly, eating from the legs up to the throat, and in this way draws out all the intestines and eats them. In nothing do the other deer associate with it, except through a foul stench that it carries.

¶The quaumiztli [tree-lion]: it lives only as the mountain lion lives, always dwelling in the treetops and in the high crags. If it eats anything, it rarely comes down to the ground.

¶The maçamiztli [deer-lion]: it is called by this name because it resembles a deer in certain ways, yet is truly like a mountain lion. The females resemble doe-deer in appearance; it has a long tail. It approaches and comes near; it is truly like a mountain lion in its nature, and none can escape it, none can flee from it once it has seized a deer. Thereupon the deer-lion tears it: it tears it open and devours it. It is extremely large and very fat. It seizes prey in its claws like iron hooks. Whatever it takes, whatever it catches, it strips off the skin, peels it entirely. It is greatly to be feared; it wanders seeking to devour, it never rests in peace.

                                    folio 7.
in the middle, in the center. And in the morning, when day breaks, it throws itself down; it rolls in the dung; it is a wildcat. And yet it knows how to recognize itself. It goes about scattering things.

There is another animal in this land called the cujtlamjztli, which means "bastard lion." According to what is said of it, it is a wolf: it eats dogs and chickens and sheep. In wintertime it secludes itself until it can no more, and then it goes about hunting for three days without stopping. For this reason they call it "bastard lion," because it is a glutton; it has no den like the lions; and at night it eats the chickens and the sheep; and even so, this beast kills all the chickens and sheep it can.

The cujtlamjztli lives in the forest, it wanders through the ravines, like the mountain lion. It goes about at night, the cujtlamjztli. It seizes animals; it hunts and captures them; it takes four, or it seizes them in its jaws. Two days, three days it goes without eating, then all at once it gorges itself; it comes down from above, and thus it is called cujtlamjztli, because it is voracious and also because it does not shelter itself. At night it then comes to eat the turkey; it is like the large wild beast. It also looks like a wildcat and also like a dog.

There is another animal called iteujn quanjs, which means "camel of dogs," which is of the same kind as the one described above. They are called by this name iteujn quanjs, or camels of dogs, because at night—

The iteujn quanjs. It is also called cujtlamjztli. At night it comes into the chicken coops. And having done that, it then—

Book Eleventh

It approaches the settlements and from nearby begins to howl; and all the dogs that hear it respond by howling, and go running to where it is. Once the dogs are together with it, they kill what is needed to eat, and it eats them; the rest go off — its food is the dogs — and it finds them very tasty. This animal, according to this account, appears to be a wolf.

Second paragraph on animals such as foxes, wolves, and other similar animals.

There is in this land an animal called coyote, which some Spaniards call a fox and others call a wolf; but according to its characteristics, it is neither wolf nor fox, but an animal proper to this land. It is very shaggy with long fur, has a thick and very woolly tail; it has small, pointed ears; its snout is long and not very thick, and dark; its legs are sinewy; its claws are curved and black. It is very alert and cautious. To hunt, it crouches down and lies in wait, looking in all directions to catch its prey. It is very cunning in ambushing its game. When it wants to rush at the prey, it first hurls itself—

[Nahuatl column:]
Coyote: it has a long, blunt snout; it is wide-faced; it has long legs, long-legged, slender-legged; it is pinched at the temples, sleek-headed, dark-throated, white-eared, white-toed; its paws are dark, it shows well, it knows things. How it hunts: it stalks crouching, it presses itself low; it rolls in the grass, it stretches itself on the ground; it sets itself thus, it crouches. It watches keenly in all directions; it knows a person from afar. It launches itself forward. It seeks sheep(?); it seizes game...

On animals.     fo. 8

its venom, against it, to infect it and discourage its spirit. This animal is diabolical: if someone takes away its prey, it takes note of them and seeks to take revenge, killing their chickens or other animals of their household. And if it notices any such thing, it waits for that person when they travel along the road, and places itself in front of them, gesturing as if it wants to eat them, to frighten them. And sometimes it also accompanies itself with three or four companions to frighten them further. They do this either by night or by day. This animal has exquisite qualities — it is grateful. Now in these times there occurred a noteworthy thing, concerning one of these little animals. A traveler, going along his road, saw one of these animals making a signal to him with its hand, that he should approach. The traveler was frightened by this, but went to where it was. And when he drew near, he saw a snake that was coiled around the neck of that animal, and had its head tucked under the armpit of that little creature, holding it very tightly. This snake was one of those called cincoatl. And the traveler

[Right column — Nahuatl:]
was watching it. And just then, like a person: when it had already called out, when it had already cried for help, it grabbed the fur from its back, so that it would come to its aid. And the heart said: it is addressing me, calling me. And if someone harms it, it will rebuke me, it will mock me, it will shame me, it will threaten me, it will terrify me: and also two, three, those it will set against you in the open field, or maybe people. And also when its spirit is restored, it is grateful, it gives thanks: as many as are gathered, it will approach them. A certain man came out onto a road in the ravine, following after his companion. And then the coyote came out onto the path ahead of them; it was very agitated and very alarmed about the companion — something was happening there. And having approached: he saw the snake, which had thrown itself upon him; it was coming out from between his legs, the snake: it was coming out from beside his ear, having wrapped itself around him: its name, cincoatl. And the traveler said: "I will help him." And then he took up his companion's walking staff.

Book Eleven

When he saw what was happening, he thought to himself, saying: "Help those people there." And he decided to help that animal; and he took up a stick and began to strike the snake. Then the snake uncoiled and fell to the ground, and began to go away and hide itself among the grass. The little animal also fled, and after a while it came back and found the traveler again, among some cornfields. It was carrying two roosters in its mouth, by their necks, and it laid them before the traveler who had been saved from the snake. It made a sign with its snout that he should take them, and it went along behind the traveler until he reached his house. When it saw where he went in, it went to look for a hen and brought it to his house. And two days later it brought a rooster to his house. This animal eats raw meat, and also dried and green ears of corn, and green stalks, and hens, and bread, and honey. This animal is caught in a trap, or with a snare, or with a lasso, or they shoot it with an arrow. They also set traps for it in the maguey plants when it goes to drink the honey.

[Nahuatl column:] It called out, it cried out; it went quickly toward the snake, going straight at it. It spread itself out — perhaps it had done something elsewhere on the road when the coyote arrived there. And then the coyote drew itself up and rolled about; perhaps it had done something elsewhere. The coyote came again. It went to its master's house. Again it went straight toward the coyote. The coyote gave it something — a turkey hen. And then it awaited its warrior companion. Again, however many times, it gave people there in the courtyard turkeys. The food of the coyote: meat, green raw [corn]; ears of corn, beans, something round, black mushrooms, tamales, tortillas, honey. And as for the ways of the coyote: it goes about marking its territory, it moves about, it wanders about, it digs around, it goes about smelling things.

Of Animals [page] 9

There is another animal of this species in this land that they call cujtlachcoiotl: it has the same qualities described above; except that in its fur it resembles the bear [cujtlachtli]: and it has a thick ruff, very fine: and on its chest and face it has a crest of large hairs, which makes it look frightening.

There is another animal of this species which they call azcatioiotl: it has the same qualities described above; except that it sits on anthills, which is why it is called azcatioiotl: and also when it howls at night it makes many voices together, some thick, others thin, others even thinner.

There is another animal of this species which they call tlalcoiotl: it has the qualities described above; but it does not live in the mountains like the others, but rather near the towns. Some call it fox or little fox. It eats chickens and beans and ears of corn, and many other things.

There is another animal called ocotochtli: which also lives among the rocks and mountains; it is the size of a small [animal], low and stout: its fur is brown along its back

[Nahuatl column:]
It is called cuetlach coiotl, or cajtla coiotl, it is like a coyote: its fur is like that of a cujtlachtli, shaggy, bristly.

The azcal coiotl is also like a coyote, and it is called azcalcoiotl because it cries out, it howls, it makes sounds like a coyote, it makes rumbling sounds, it whistles, it makes small sounds.

The tlalcoiotl: its name is tlalcoiotl, it lives near houses, it is not raised among the crags, it wanders nearby: it is not a far-ranging coyote, it lives around the settlements, it goes about eating birds, it eats turkeys, it eats ears of corn, it eats cinquefoil berries: it eats all kinds of things, it eats snakes.

The ocotochtli: smoky-colored, whitish-gray, its back [described further below]

Book Eleven

and on the belly whitish, with some black spots, sparse and small: it has soft fur, it has a round head, and small ears, like those of a cat: it has a round face: a short snout from which comes a rough or thorny tongue: it has a thin call like a high-pitched string, it is very agile and leaps greatly as though it flies. This animal has a singular and special property by which it hunts to feed other fierce beasts — it hunts men or deer or other animals. It hunts in this manner: seeing that what it wishes to hunt is approaching, it hides behind a tree; and when the prey arrives, it launches itself, rushes at it, and sprays its tongue into the eyes, and it is so venomous that it kills at once; as the animal or person it has killed falls, it covers it with leaves and climbs up into a tree and begins to howl, whose howling can be heard from very far away; and then the other fierce beasts such as tigers, lions, etc., who hear that howl, immediately understand that they are being called to eat, and they come to where the ocotochili is, and they see the prey, and the first thing they do is drink the blood; and afterward they tear it apart and eat it: and through all of this, the ocotochili stands apart, watching how the others eat.

[Nahuatl column:] White on the belly, slender-necked, smoke-colored on the throat; on its back dark, ocelot-colored, ocelot-spotted, resembling an ocelot, of a tawny hue, of a tan hue, wide, fluffy, with a rough nape: small and round, plump in body: meaty and round-headed; with small ears, small-cheeked, with a blunt little muzzle, with small round lips, with a prickly tongue, making a sound toward those it encounters. It is very swift, it springs forward, it leaps, it flies: its body is like a rabbit's; it is fierce, among those that devour. In this way it hunts, its function, what it does when it sees either an animal or a person: then something strikes it, it goes around behind a tree, somehow it goes around behind. And when it arrives behind the tree, it crouches down watching, it peers at it, it goes forward to face it. And the animal or person, then its eyes are blinded, it cannot help itself: and then it weeps in pain. And the blood [flows]: then it howls toward it, calling out...

Concerning Animals.          folio 10.

And after they have eaten, it eats what is left over; and they say that it does this because it has such a poisonous tongue, that if it were to eat, it would poison the flesh, and the other beasts would die from eating it.

There is another small animal they call ostoca: it is called by this name because it always lives in caves and gives birth to its young there. It is very small, has a snout like a little pig, has somewhat long and slightly rough fur, and is of a dark brown color. It eats mice and squirrels and also eats rabbits.

There is another small animal they call mapachitli, and they also call it cioatlamacazqui, and it is also called ilamatan, which means "little old woman." It has hands and feet like a person; it destroys the cornfields when the ears are still green by eating them; it climbs the trees

[Nahuatl column:]
pitzao: and it makes a piercing sound, it shows itself on the road, then it goes ahead quickly, and they will eat it. And they came forward then quickly, it went down, and it went down into mietlan, and there it nurses its young, it is cradled; and some go down it as well; then afterward they will take it down and tear it apart.

Ostooa: it is also called ostooa, it always goes about seeking caves, in the cave it makes its home, there it descends, there it crawls about; thus its beak is like a small thin bill; it is thin-necked, wide-bodied, large-cheeked; it eats small fish, and in water it feeds on small fish, it carries them into shallow water and swallows them there.

Mapachitli: it is also called cioatlamacazqui, and also called ilamaton; the mapachitli is so named because it is truly just like a person in its hands; it does not sleep, its hands are like a human hand; then it reaches into the cornfield with them.

Book Eleven

...and it eats the fruit of those trees and eats the honey of the maguey plants, and it lives in caves. It makes its home in the mountains, in the rocky crags, and among the water reeds. In wintertime, when there are no fruits or other such things, it eats rats and other vermin. Sometimes it walks on two feet like a person, and other times on four feet like an animal. It steals whatever it finds, being by nature thieving, and because it has hands like a person, they call it Mapachitli. It is short and stocky, and has long fur; its tail is long, rough, and hairy, after the manner of an opossum. Its head is large, its ears small. Its snout is long, slender, and dark; its body is gray and hairy.

Another little animal called Yecotli is like the Mapachitli described above, except that it has no hands or feet like a person, only like an animal. It is gray in color. It is called Pacotli, as if one were to say...

[Nahuatl column:] ...it climbs trees, it goes up the ceiba tree, it eats capulin berries and sour fruits... it lives in caves, on rocky ledges, in ravines, in water, in reeds... it moves about... it makes itself heard... they call it Mapachitli... it steals... its tail is bushy, broad... it is called tlacaxoopale, pachtontli... its tail is disheveled, divided, hanging... it makes a sound...

Pecotli: It is just like [the one described], it has no hands like a person, it is dark-colored. It is called Pecotli because it is good to eat, it is food...

Of Animals. Folio 11.

[The animal is called] glutton, because it eats all things, and always eats, never becomes satisfied.
